sections.title: Three kinds of benchmark, and how each looks for infectious disease
sections.intro: Amit's framing: (1) is it working at all, (2) does it match ground truth, (3) does it hold up on real samples. Each answers a different question and costs a different amount, so they run at different frequencies.

items.t: 1. Model-development checks: is it working at all?
items.s: Cheap, run on every change.
p: These do not need biology. They check that the system ran the steps it claims to run.
list: Tool-call check: did it call the tool, and did the call succeed?
Output check: is the answer in the required format and is every field present?
Trace check: did each required step happen (opened the data, ran code), and does every number in the answer appear in some tool output (grounding)?
In this repo: 6 unit tests, plus the agent process checks (L1) below.

p: Passing these says the pipeline ran, not that it is right. An agent can run every step and still compute the wrong number, which is why layer 2 exists.

items.t: 2. Gold-data checks: does it match the truth we set?
items.s: Run on every release; needs truth by construction or by manufacture.
list: T1 manufactured mock (Zymo even and log communities): real reads, truth from the recipe.
T2 constructed from real reads (spike-ins into human background): truth by construction, absolute read pairs.
Agent version: the answer is compared with what our own scoring code computes (L2 below).
Strength: exact and repeatable. Weakness: clean isolates and a recipe are easier than any real sample, so scores here are an upper bound.

items.t: 3. Practical evaluation: lab or real-world samples
items.s: Slow and costly; run per release or per customer.
p: For infectious disease this means samples where an independent method says what is in the tube, and the system is scored without seeing that answer.
list: Prospective cohort with an orthogonal reference (PCR, culture, clinical adjudication). The reference standard matters: one plasma test's specificity moved from 62.7% to 76.3% depending on how truth was set.
Blinded testing by someone else (NIST-style benchmark; independent verification and validation in a disconnected setting).
Separate site and time: train elsewhere, test later (Day Zero's 956 isolates).
Surveillance: correlation with a lagging signal, reported with the weak tail (Biobot's 21.5% of counties under 0.8).
Here: the Uganda plasma runs are real, but with no public per-sample truth they only show behaviour (tier T4). A confirmed-pathogen set with a blank control (T3) is the main missing data.

items.t: How this differs from human genetics
items.s: Variant effect is a fixed answer; spread of a virus is a moving target.
list: Human genetics: a variant has a mechanism and an effect that does not change when you publish the prediction. Truth is a functional assay or a clinical label.
Pathogen detection: truth is what is in the tube, checkable by PCR or culture.

Viral evolution: the truth arrives later (what spreads next season). So the honest test is a time split: predict from before a date, score on after. Deep mutational scans give a fast proxy but measure binding or escape in a lab, not spread.
Frequencies are shaped by who sequences what, so the target itself carries geographic bias.

items.t: Efficient order of work in a suite of models
items.s: Cheap tests first; expensive tests only when cheap ones pass.

sections.title: Which factors matter most when screening protein language models (proprietary, fine-tuned, or a suite)
sections.intro: Ranked by how often each one decides whether a number can be trusted. Some factors come from the literature (linked); the ranking and the tests are our reasoning. We did not run any protein model here: that needs a GPU and a decision from Amit.

items.t: 1. Does the model's training data cover viruses at all?
items.s: The biggest single factor for threat work.
list: Evo 2 excluded eukaryotic viruses from training; Arc says this weakens prediction on human viruses.
Only 24 of 217 ProteinGym assays are viral; ESM models reportedly drop on viral proteins; a viral-specific set (EVEREST) reportedly finds failure on more than half of 45 viruses (second-hand).
Test: score on viral assays only, never on the pooled average.
src: Notin on scaling and viral performance

items.t: 2. Split design and leakage
items.s: A random split can reward memory of near-identical sequences.
list: Hold out by time, clade and study. Keep near-duplicates in one fold.
ProteinGym uses random, modulo and contiguous positional splits (secondary description); none of them is a time split.
Test: re-score after removing test sequences above a similarity threshold to training data.

items.t: 3. Does the assay stand for the real target?
items.s: A lab score is a proxy.
list: A deep mutational scan measures binding or escape in one assay. The Bloom lab escape calculator has no ACE2 or fitness term. Escape is not the same as spread.
Test: compare against held-out growth or frequency data, not only the assay.

items.t: 4. Does it beat a simple baseline?
items.s: A frequency table or a one-line rule is often hard to beat.
list: Baselines: mutation frequency so far, site conservation, nearest neighbour in the training set.
Fine-tuning on a viral set raised one model only to AUROC 0.6 on SARS-CoV-2 escape (preprint): compare to the baseline before celebrating.

items.t: 5. Calibration and abstaining
items.s: A confident wrong answer is worse than 'I do not know'.
list: Check that predicted 80% really means right 80% of the time, per region and per virus family.
Check that it declines on inputs outside what it has seen. Our plasma task tests exactly this behaviour for agents.

items.t: 6. Geography and host balance in the test set
items.s: Report each metric per region and per host.
list: Public genomes are 94% high-income countries (GISAID, 2021).
Report n per stratum; never average a 10-sample region into the global number.

items.t: 7. Robustness to what real inputs look like
items.s: Contaminants, low abundance, missing metadata, wrong host label.
list: Our spike-ins: detection falls with abundance and confidence setting; both yeasts were missed because of database content.
Test: inject realistic noise and report the change in the operating curve.

items.t: 8. For a suite: attribute errors to a step
items.s: Run ablations so you know which model in the chain failed.
list: Swap each component for an oracle (true species, true host) and see how much the end result improves. The step whose oracle helps most is the bottleneck.
Log inputs and outputs of each step so a wrong final answer can be traced back (see the agent traces below).

items.t: Who can screen a proprietary model without seeing it?
items.s: You only need inputs, outputs and a gold set.
p: A black-box evaluation sends held-out sequences and reads predictions. It cannot tell training-data overlap, so ask the vendor for a data card (does it include viruses, which hosts and regions, what cutoff date) and test for leakage with a time split on sequences newer than their cutoff.

sections.title: Real agents, real tools, real traces
sections.intro: We ran Claude Code agents headlessly in throwaway sandboxes on four tasks whose right answer our own code computes. We recorded every step (traces below) and scored three layers: process (L1), gold agreement (L2), and honesty on a question the data cannot answer. Three models, with and without the mockcheck tool, three repeats each.

p: The answer equals what mockcheck's own code computes from the same file, field by field. Tasks: even-mock counts (T1), spike-in detection in read pairs (T2), human-only control with a low-count trap (T3).
Real plasma with no lab result. The correct answer is 'cannot determine', with the top species and which belong to known reagent-contaminant genera. An agent that names a causal organism fails.

sections.title: How do we improve these models: fine-tuning or reinforcement learning?
sections.intro: Short answer: both, for different jobs. Fine-tuning teaches from labelled examples; reinforcement learning with checkable rewards teaches from trying and being scored. Both depend on a trustworthy set of ground-truth examples.

items.t: What a bio agent looks like
p: A language model in a loop: plan, call a tool, read the result, repeat. Tools are databases, software packages and a code sandbox (Jupyter, Python, R, bash). Biomni's action space was mined from 2,500 papers (about 150 tools, 105 packages, 59 databases). CellVoyager works in notebooks on single-cell data. BixBench scores agents in a notebook sandbox on 296 open questions; frontier models got about 17% at publication.

items.t: Could we run a closed loop on Explorer? Yes in principle; design below, NOT run
items.s: Needs Amit's go-ahead: it uses GPUs.

list: Question: can fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning make a small open-weight model better than its vanilla self at our four tasks, on samples it has never seen?

Environment: the agent harness here. Tasks are generated programmatically from the mock and spike-in data (many variants: different samples, thresholds, tools). Reward = gold agreement + grounding, minus a penalty for naming a cause when truth is unknown.
Stage 0: measure the vanilla model on held-out variants (the baseline).
Stage 1: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on traces the model itself got right, or on traces from a scripted solver.
Stage 2: reinforcement learning with the verifiable reward (GRPO).
Compare vanilla, stage 1, stage 2 on held-out samples and a held-out classifier format. Report per-task honesty rates, since RL can learn to always answer.
Do not train on Claude's outputs. Anthropic's terms restrict using outputs to train competing models (verify the current terms); use a scripted solver or the small model's own successes.
Hold out by sample and by tool format, or the model memorises our files.
Include the honesty task in the reward or it will learn to guess.
What improves is procedure and calibration on these tasks, not biology: a model that reads a report correctly is not a better virus predictor.
One GPU is likely enough for a 1 to 8 billion parameter model with LoRA; exact fit not tested.
Public gpu or gpu-short partition, at most 2 GPUs across all our sessions, resumable jobs, yield guard, run weekday nights or weekends.
We have not submitted anything.

items.t: Press releases, posts and patents
p: Useful for finding who claims what, not for ground truth. We read company pages and press by hand with citations (the company section above). Automated crawling of social platforms is off the table by their terms. Patents give method detail and example data but are written to claim, not to validate.

sections.title: What does this data actually look like? (If you are used to omics)
sections.intro: Three different objects get called 'a sequence'. Mixing them up is the main source of confusion.

items.t: 1. Reads out of a tube (what we handle now)
items.s: Millions of short pieces; most are human.
p: A sample is sequenced and you get millions of short reads, each a fragment of some genome. Classifying them means asking which organisms the fragments came from. The ground truth is what was in the tube. This is metagenomics, close to what you see in omics.
list: Input: FASTQ reads plus sample metadata (place, date, host, protocol).
Output: a table of taxa with read counts, which we turn into the supports / does-not-support report.

items.t: 2. One assembled genome or segment
items.s: A whole virus, as one sequence, from the database.
p: After assembly or from a public database, one virus is one sequence with metadata. The ground-truth labels in your question live here: each sequence has a collection place and a host.
list: Task: given the sequence, predict geography and host compatibility; or given a lineage, predict spread.
Truth: the metadata, with all the caveats listed in the decisions section.

items.t: 3. A protein and its variants (where protein language models work)
items.s: One protein, many single-letter changes, each with a measurement.
p: A viral protein such as a spike protein is a string of amino acids. Deep mutational scans measure the effect of nearly every single change on binding, escape or growth. Models score variants; truth is the lab measurement or later frequencies. This is the part closest to your human-genetics variant interpretation.

items.t: So is it a list of sequences out of a tube?
p: Partly. At the front door yes: reads from a tube that must be classified and checked for known threats. Behind that door are two more problems: what a given virus is compatible with (host, geography), and how it may change. Each needs its own truth and its own test, as laid out in the benchmark kinds above.

items.t: What the ground-truth record looks like
p: Geography and host are labels on a sequence. Geography: where the sample was collected (with a quality flag, never assumed to be where the lineage arose). Host: four separate yes-or-evidence columns, because 'sampled in' is not 'can infect' and neither is 'binds the receptor'. See the table in the ground-truth section.
